contentStatus: Educational summaries; no clinical protocol or NASA approval. Feature mappings are AstroCare design decisions.

sources.title: Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight
sources.summary: NASA organizes human spaceflight challenges into five interacting hazards.

sources.title: Risks of Human Spaceflight
sources.summary: Spaceflight can affect circulation, balance, immunity, nutrition and other aspects of health. Effects differ by mission destination.

sources.title: Ongoing HRP Research in Space
sources.summary: NASA describes investigations including ARCHeR, which monitored activity, sleep and wellbeing, and Standard Measures, which collects consistent physiological and psychological information.
sources.feature: Sleep history, consistent check-ins and research cards

sources.title: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health
sources.summary: The Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer is being developed for continuous, autonomous neutron-radiation measurements. The article discusses instrumentation, not a live data service.
sources.feature: Radiation education beside explicitly simulated instrument readings

sources.title: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
sources.summary: Space experiments support deep-space preparation and knowledge that can benefit health on Earth. Longer missions face communication delays and reduced access to supplies and emergency medical assistance.
sources.feature: Offline design rationale and Space-to-Earth section

sources.title: Pulse
sources.agency: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine
sources.summary: A pulse can be counted at the wrist. Activity and measurement context matter when comparing readings.
sources.type: General education, not a spaceflight procedure

sources.title: Temperature measurement
sources.agency: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine
sources.summary: Temperature can help identify illness. Measurement method and recent activity, eating or drinking affect interpretation.
sources.type: General education, not a spaceflight procedure

sources.title: Home Blood Pressure Monitoring
sources.summary: Validated upper-arm devices, appropriate cuffs, quiet rest and consistent positioning support reliable home measurements.
sources.type: Earth-based education, not a microgravity protocol

sources.title: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings
sources.summary: Blood pressure categories for adults: normal below 120/80 mmHg, elevated 120-129 systolic, stage 1 130-139 or 80-89, stage 2 at or above 140 or 90 mmHg.
sources.feature: Reference-range layer of the monitoring engine (systolic and diastolic flags)
sources.type: Earth adult reference ranges, not microgravity-specific

sources.title: About Sleep
sources.summary: Adults generally need 7 or more hours of sleep per night; insufficient sleep affects health and performance.
sources.feature: Sleep reference flags (under 6 h watch, under 4.5 h alert)

sources.title: Blood glucose test
sources.agency: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine
sources.summary: Fasting blood glucose of 70-99 mg/dL is the usual normal range; values below 70 mg/dL are low. Meal timing changes interpretation.
sources.feature: Glucose reference flags and the requirement to record fasting or meal context

sources.title: OSD-575: Inspiration4 comprehensive metabolic panel
sources.summary: Blood chemistry from the four civilian Inspiration4 crew at three pre-flight and four post-flight timepoints, with laboratory reference ranges.
sources.feature: Spaceflight biomarker explorer: per-crew trajectories and change from each person's own pre-flight baseline

sources.title: Measurements of energetic particle radiation in transit to Mars on the Mars Science Laboratory
sources.summary: The RAD instrument measured an average dose-equivalent rate of about 1.84 mSv per day inside the spacecraft during cruise to Mars.
sources.feature: Mars-transit dose rate in the radiation mission planner

sources.title: Mars' surface radiation environment measured with the Mars Science Laboratory's Curiosity rover
sources.summary: Curiosity's RAD measured an average dose-equivalent rate of about 0.64 mSv per day on the Martian surface.
sources.feature: Mars-surface dose rate in the radiation mission planner

sources.title: First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface
sources.summary: Chang'e 4's Lunar Lander Neutron and Dosimetry experiment measured a dose-equivalent rate of about 1.37 mSv per day on the lunar surface.
sources.feature: Lunar-surface dose rate in the radiation mission planner

sources.title: PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2012
sources.summary: Open ICU dataset of 8,000 stays with time-stamped vital signs. AstroCare trains next-observation forecasters on heart rate, blood pressure and temperature.
sources.feature: Live-monitor forecast models and their conformal expected-range bands

sources.title: Maximizing sensitivity of the psychomotor vigilance test (PVT) to sleep loss
sources.summary: Defines the brief 3-minute PVT (PVT-B): 2-5 s random intervals, lapses as responses of 355 ms or longer, and shows it remains sensitive to sleep loss.
sources.feature: Cognitive performance module: test protocol, lapse threshold and scoring

sources.title: Development and validation of the Cognition test battery for spaceflight
sources.agency: Basner et al., Aerospace Medicine and Human Performance (2015)
sources.summary: Describes a 10-test cognitive battery, including a PVT, designed for astronauts and used in spaceflight research.
sources.feature: Rationale for repeated cognitive self-tests on long missions

hazards.title: Space radiation
hazards.summary: Radiation is invisible and presents a major spaceflight hazard.
hazards.monitoring: Explore simulated instrument history. Ordinary vital signs do not measure radiation exposure.

hazards.title: Isolation and confinement
hazards.summary: Long periods in confined groups can affect behavior and teamwork.
hazards.monitoring: Record sleep and self-reported mood; these are observations, not a mental-health diagnosis.

hazards.title: Distance from Earth
hazards.summary: Medical care, advice and supplies become harder to obtain farther from Earth.
hazards.monitoring: Keep guidance and records available offline. Export a handover for later communication.

hazards.title: Changing gravity
hazards.summary: Muscles, bones, balance and internal organs adapt to different gravity conditions.
hazards.monitoring: Log symptoms and measurement context. Routine vital signs do not quantify bone density.

hazards.title: Hostile and closed environments
hazards.summary: Spacecraft must manage conditions including temperature, pressure, noise and microbial communities.
hazards.monitoring: Track observations and symptoms. Cabin conditions require dedicated environmental sensors.

measurements.title: Heart rate
measurements.why: A consistent pulse history describes cardiovascular observations; it does not identify their cause.
instructions: For a resting reading, rest first and record recent activity.
Place the index and middle fingers under the opposite wrist, below the thumb base.
Count beats for one full minute and record the result and time.
measurements.scope: General education; use mission-approved procedures in flight.

measurements.title: Blood pressure
measurements.why: NASA studies cardiovascular adaptation in weightlessness. Record both values and measurement context.
instructions: Earth training example: use a validated upper-arm monitor with the correct cuff size.
Rest quietly for at least five minutes; place the cuff on bare skin and support the arm at heart level.
Follow device instructions; take two readings one minute apart and record each.
measurements.scope: Earth-based guidance. These posture instructions are not validated microgravity procedures.

measurements.title: Body temperature
measurements.why: Temperature can help assess illness; measurement method affects comparisons.
instructions: Use a digital thermometer and follow its cleaning and operating instructions.
For oral measurement, position the probe under the tongue, close the mouth and wait for the device signal.
Record the site, value and time. Recent exercise, food and hot or cold drinks may affect readings.
measurements.scope: General education; follow the mission-approved device procedure.

measurements.title: Sleep duration
measurements.why: NASA's ARCHeR research includes sleep, activity and wellbeing observations.
instructions: Enter estimated total sleep during the previous 24 hours.
Use the same reporting window each time.
Mark this as self-report, not a wearable measurement.
measurements.scope: AstroCare reporting convention, not a validated questionnaire.

measurements.title: Mood check-in
measurements.why: Wellbeing observations can support conversations about how someone feels.
instructions: Choose the rating that best matches how you feel now.
Add context in your own words.
This app-designed scale does not diagnose a condition.

measurements.title: Blood glucose
measurements.why: Record a measured glucose value together with the method and fasting or meal context. Research forecasts do not diagnose a condition.
instructions: Use the mission-approved glucose device and follow its instructions.
Check that the device uses mg/dL before entering a reading; do not enter mmol/L in this field.
Record the time, device, measurement method and fasting or meal context. Do not change medication based on this prototype.
measurements.scope: AstroCare logging convention; NASA risks motivate the feature but do not provide a glucose measurement or treatment protocol.

researchCards.title: Sleep and wellbeing
researchCards.text: ARCHeR investigated wellbeing, activity and sleep. It motivates consistent self-reports, but does not validate AstroCare alerts.

researchCards.title: Consistent observations
researchCards.text: Standard Measures collects physiological and psychological information. AstroCare preserves units, time and provenance for understandable histories.

researchCards.title: Space to Earth
researchCards.text: Offline logging and clear explanations could be explored for remote communities. This is a proposed application, not a demonstrated clinical benefit.

emergencyBoundary: The five challenge resources are not complete emergency treatment protocols. Use an explicitly labelled observation-and-handover simulation until a mission-appropriate protocol is verified and reviewed. Do not invent medication, CPR, oxygen or evacuation steps. No observations are transmitted unless transport is implemented.
radiationBoundary: No live sensor is connected. Synthetic numbers illustrate interface behavior only. Do not claim CANS data, radiation prediction, clinical dose limits or conversion between absorbed and equivalent dose without a justified model.
